# Sample and taxa tibble
<center>
![](images/table_3.png){style="width:200px; background: white; border: white solid 5px; border-radius: 5px"}
</center>

The first step is to extract the genus abundance table and then transpose it.

Transposing is vital for the next step as it means that:

- Each column is a taxa (except the Sample column)
- Each row is a sample

## Transposed genus abundance
<center>
![](images/transpose_table.png){style="width:400px; background: white; border-radius:5px"}
</center>

Carry out aggregation and transposing.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#Abundance tibble of samples (rows) against genera (columns)
genus_tibble  <- pseq |>
	#Aggregate to genus
	microbiome::aggregate_taxa("Genus", verbose = FALSE) |>
	#Extract otu_table
	phyloseq::otu_table() |>
	#Convert to data.frame and transpose
	as.data.frame() |> t() |>
	#Convert to tibble
	dplyr::as_tibble(rownames = "Sample")
#Display top 6 rows of tibble
head(genus_tibble)
```

## Tibbles and transposing

You may notice that we do not use the function `microbiome::otu_tibble()` in the above code.
This is because transposing a __tibble__ will convert our tibble into a transposed matrix rather than a transposed tibble.
This matrix has our column names in the first row which we do not want.
Therefore, it is easier to go from phyloseq -> otu_table -> data.frame -> transposed -> tibble.
Annoyingly complex but 

If you want to see this in action you can type and run the below demonstrative code.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#Demonstration on why we don't use microibome::otu_tibble()
pseq |>
	#Aggregate to genus
	microbiome::aggregate_taxa("Genus", verbose = FALSE) |>
	#Extract otu_table as a tibble
	microbiome::otu_tibble() |>
	#Transpose
	t() |>
	#View top 6 rows
	head()
```
